Hind bint Utba, who once wished the Prophet's family degraded, now wishes it honoured; he lets her feed her children from miserly Abu Sufyan's property only what is reasonable.
Before Islam, Zaid bin Amr bin Nufail refuses meat slaughtered for idols, turns from Jewish and Christian scholars to Abraham's religion, and saves little girls from being killed.
Carrying stones to rebuild the Ka'bah, the Prophet falls unconscious on removing his waist sheet; there was no wall around the Ka'bah until Umar built one, raised by Ibn Az-Zubair.
Before Islam people fasted Ashura, shunned Umrah in the Hajj months, swore by their fathers, stood for funerals and left Muzdalifa after sunrise; the Prophet kept or changed some.
The Prophet praises a verse of Labid and forbids selling an unborn camel's offspring; Abu Bakr vomits food earned by fortune-telling, and Abu Talib settles a killing by Qasama.
Inspired at forty, the Prophet in Mecca tells the persecuted Khabbab earlier believers endured worse; Uqba lays entrails on him and throttles him, and the first converts were few.
A tree told the Prophet of the jinn who heard the Quran; he tells Abu Huraira not to bring bones or dung for cleaning, as they are the jinn's food.
Abu Dhar sends his brother to Mecca, then comes himself, is led to the Prophet by Ali, embraces Islam, and is beaten for proclaiming it until Al-Abbas rescues him.
Before his Islam Umar tied Sa'id bin Zaid to make him leave Islam; when Umar converts, Al-As bin Wail protects him from the crowd, and Umar questions a former foreteller.
When the Meccans ask for a miracle, the moon splits in two with Hira between the halves, and at Mina the Prophet tells those with him to bear witness.
Urged to punish his brother Al-Walid, Uthman recalls his two migrations and loyalty to the Prophet, Abu Bakr and Umar, and has Al-Walid flogged forty lashes.
On the emigrants to Ethiopia: the Prophet condemns pictures and worship places over graves seen there, no longer answers greetings in prayer, and gives the ship's people two migrations.
The Prophet announces the Negus's death the day he dies, calls him a pious man and a brother, and leads his funeral prayer in rows with four Takbir.
Setting out for Hunain, the Prophet plans to camp at Khaif Bani Kinana, where the pagans swore to boycott Banu Hashim.
Dying, Abu Talib holds to Abdul Muttalib's religion; a verse forbids seeking forgiveness for pagans, and the Prophet says thanks to him Abu Talib is in a shallow fire.
When Quraysh disbelieve him, Allah shows the Prophet Jerusalem to describe; he recounts his heart washed, the Buraq, prophets in seven heavens and fifty prayers reduced to five.
Ka'b bin Malik, Jabir and his uncles attended the Aqaba pledge, where, Ubada says, they pledged to worship Allah alone and avoid theft, illegal sexual intercourse, killing and slander.
Aisha tells of being engaged to the Prophet at six and handed to him at nine in Medina; he twice saw her pictured on silk in a dream.
Khabbab says the emigrants' reward is with Allah, recalling Mus'ab's short shroud; emigration counts by intention, ended with Mecca's conquest, and the Prophet lived ten years as an emigrant.
The Prophet tells of a slave choosing what is with Allah over this world; Abu Bakr weeps, is praised for his companionship and wealth, and only his door stays open.
Abu Bakr gives up Ibn ad-Daghina's protection and migrates with the Prophet via Thaur's cave; Suraqa's horse sinks; Asma's son is born at Quba; Abdullah bin Salam accepts Islam.
Umar's grants to early Emigrants; Khabbab on Emigrants who died unrewarded in this world, like Mus'ab; Umar's hope for their deeds with the Prophet; Ibn Umar pledging before his father.
Abu Bakr recounts the journey, milk from a shepherd and hiding in the cave; he kisses feverish Aisha, dyes his hair, divorces Um Bakr; a bedouin asks about migrating.
The first Emigrants and the Prophet reach Medina; he prays for its love and health; Uthman's two migrations; Medina, place of migration and Sunna; Ansar lodge Emigrants by lot.
The day of Bu'ath before the mission divided the tribes and killed their nobles, easing their conversion; girls sing Ansar songs of Bu'ath on Eid, and the Prophet allows it.
The Prophet's mosque is built; Emigrants get three days in Mecca after Hajj; his arrival starts the calendar; prayer becomes four rak'at except travelling; he prays their migration be fulfilled.
The Prophet makes Abdur-Rahman bin Auf and Sa'd bin ar-Rabi' brothers; Abdur-Rahman declines half Sa'd's property, trades, marries an Ansari woman and is told to give a banquet.
Abdullah bin Salam asks the Prophet three things only a prophet can answer, accepts Islam, and the Jews who praised him call him the most wicked among them.
Al-Bara and Zaid bin Arqam say the Prophet allowed selling dirhams hand to hand but not on credit.
The Prophet says had ten Jews believed, all would have; he orders fasting Ashura as they did, wears his hair loose like them, then parts it; they divided the Scripture.
Salman al-Farisi says he was sold from master to master more than ten times, comes from Ram-Hurmuz, and puts six hundred years between Jesus and Muhammad.
Zaid bin Arqam says the Prophet made nineteen expeditions, seventeen of them with him, the first being al-Ashira.
Warned by Sa'd, Umaiya bin Khalaf is urged out by Abu Jahl and killed at Badr; Ka'b missed Badr unblamed; al-Miqdad pledges to fight; the Prophet appeals to Allah.
Al-Bara and Ibn Umar were too young for Badr, whose warriors numbered over three hundred and ten, like the believers who crossed the river with Saul.
The Prophet invokes evil on Quraysh leaders, later seen dead; Ibn Mas'ud finds Abu Jahl dying, struck down by the two sons of Afra, and hears his last words.
The verse on two disputing opponents came down about six who fought at Badr: Hamza, Ali, Ubaida, Shaiba, Utba and al-Walid; Ali duelled in two armours.
Umaiya and his son die at Badr; an old man who would not prostrate is later killed as a disbeliever; Az-Zubair's Badr and Yarmuk wounds and his dented, silver-decorated sword.
The Prophet addresses the Quraysh dead thrown into a Badr well, saying they hear him; Aisha says his words were that they now know, and Ibn Abbas explains verse 14:28.
Haritha, martyred at Badr, is in Firdaus; Hatib, a Badr warrior, is spared over his letter; arrows are used sparingly; Badr and Uhud losses; Afra's sons knock down Abu Jahl.
Ten scouts under Asim bin Thabit are surrounded by Banu Lihyan; Asim falls, Khubaib, sold in Mecca, prays two rak'at before he is killed, and wasps guard Asim's body.
